title: Tetraplegic man controls a four-limb exoskeleton and avatar through an adaptive epidural ECoG decoder at Clinatec, Grenoble
summary: A 28-year-old with C4-C5 tetraplegia cortically controlled simulated walking and 8-DoF arm movements over 24 months (Lancet Neurology 2019).
account: A 28-year-old man with tetraplegia after a C4-C5 spinal cord injury received two wireless epidural recorders of 64 electrodes each over the sensorimotor cortex. He was implanted at the Clinatec research center of the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), associated with Grenoble University Hospital. Epidural electrocorticographic signals were processed online by an adaptive decoding algorithm. It sent commands to a virtual avatar or a four-limb exoskeleton. Between 12 June 2017 and 21 July 2019 he cortically controlled a walking simulation and bimanual upper-limb movements with eight degrees of freedom. Success was 64.0% using the avatar at home and 70.9% with the exoskeleton in the laboratory. Decoding models were reusable for about seven weeks without recalibration (Lancet Neurology, 2019).
purpose: Restore mobility to people with tetraplegia by decoding brain signals to drive an exoskeleton
system: Clinatec epidural wireless brain-machine interface with adaptive decoder driving a four-limb exoskeleton and virtual avatar
developer: CEA-Clinatec (public research institute, not a company) with Grenoble University Hospital
deployer: Clinatec research center / Grenoble University Hospital clinical trial
taxonomy_note: The gain is brain-controlled exoskeleton and avatar movement for a man with tetraplegia in a proof-of-concept setting, not everyday use.

ratings.reason: One identifiable participant gained brain-controlled walking simulation and eight-degree-of-freedom arm control, exercised at home with an avatar and in the lab with the exoskeleton. It did not yet provide everyday mobility.
Single-patient proof of concept for semi-invasive long-term BCI. No population effect.

ai_role.statement: The adaptive decoding algorithm converts epidural ECoG into effector commands. The same group later described it as a recursive exponentially weighted Markov-switching multilinear mixture-of-experts model. Without it the implants record only. The exoskeleton itself was ceiling-suspended in the laboratory.

produced_by: Chronic bilateral epidural ECoG recorders with wireless transmission
Adaptive, incrementally trained decoder with idle-state support
Progressive training on mental tasks over 24 months
must_hold: Stable epidural signal quality over years
Decoder recalibration roughly every seven weeks
Laboratory suspension system for safe exoskeleton walking

fields.account: A 28-year-old man with tetraplegia after a C4-C5 spinal cord injury received two wireless epidural recorders of 64 electrodes each over the sensorimotor cortex. He was implanted at the Clinatec research center of the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), associated with Grenoble University Hospital. Epidural electrocorticographic signals were processed online by an adaptive decoding algorithm. It sent commands to a virtual avatar or a four-limb exoskeleton. Between 12 June 2017 and 21 July 2019 he cortically controlled a walking simulation and bimanual upper-limb movements with eight degrees of freedom. Success was 64.0% using the avatar at home and 70.9% with the exoskeleton in the laboratory. Decoding models were reusable for about seven weeks without recalibration (Lancet Neurology, 2019).
